###### suggestion
Let me describe current situation briefly. We have marker providers which push their markers to markerService. Markers land in 2-d storage divided by `owner`, which is a language sign, and `resource`, which is uri (or its path). This is fine until we get into situation when more that one marker provider manages markers of the same owner+resource, such as in `typescript-language-features` extension and `tsc problem-matcher`. This makes a collision, where one may overwrite each other markers inside markerService, and as it seems to me, it is the main reason of making [WatchingProblemCollector](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L412) to repush markers on textModel dispose, and also along with [StartStopProblemCollector](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L359) to filter their pushes by the textModel opened/closed status, like here [if (shouldApplyMatch)](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/common/problemCollectors.ts#L392). So, problem matchers filter their outputs based on the **assumption** that there may be other marker provider active, to not mess with it. This mechanic is not bulletproof and may create more issues in the future if more marker providers appear, and this already creates issue in the scenario discussed there. So this is the first thing we change - we let marker providers push their data to markerService without collision preventing workarounds, by adding a `origin` tag in addition to `owner` and `resource`. `origin` entity is already added by @dbaeumer https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/251268#issuecomment-3024704155, https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/253368, and now we can take it to the more substantive usage with some adjustments. For now, `origin` is `string | undefined` and is set as string for the markers originated from extension host, and undefined for everything else.

So, the first is - we removing repushes of markers by `WatchingProblemCollector` on textModel dispose, and remove their outputs filtering based on textModel existence. Simply push any marker updates to `markerService`. This significantly simplifies the update logic for marker providers

Now, the essence of suggestion is `markerService` improvement to make it able to switch active origin (naming is under the question, it may be named `visible/presenting/facadeOrigin`,  but for now I just called it `activeOrigin`), which means that [MarkerService.read](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/platform/markers/common/markerService.ts#L332) called for `owner` and `resource` outputs only markers for active origin, and triggers [onMarkerChanged](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a5914335df0bf1cae7d818a168ef321def9f8572/src/vs/platform/markers/common/markerService.ts#L158) event for updates of active origin markers only. Updates of other origins for the given owner+resource are still served, but they land to '`backyard`' storage, not visible in output and don't fire onMarkerChanged events

Thats it, it s actually simple idea. I may be unaware of impossibility of this change, but at a first glance, I like how it works. What do we get if we implement it:
1. Marker providers update pushes simplification
2. Markers storage is always up to date
3. Active origin switch is instant
4. Origin can be turned into more complex object with a hierarchy structure in the future, which may include origins prioritization logics. For example, for now we have only two priority levels - problem matchers (and maybe something else), for which we can leave origin as undefined for now, and a extension diagnostics level, which is more prioritized. There could be more levels between these two in the future, lets say we have a problem matcher diagnostics as a lowest one, then if there is some language service pushes markers it may have higher priority, and a language extension even more prioritized when a document is presented for editing. When document is removed from ui, markerService switch activeOrigin to another, language service in this case. If language service disappears, it switches to undefined origin, which is problem matchers atm. Probably too many words used to explain simple prioritization mechanics =)

I’m currently working on the implementation for pod-level resource limits defaulting, based on the guidance that pod-level limits should be derived from aggregated container limits **only when**:

1. Pod-level resource requests are explicitly set, and
2. All containers in the pod have resource limits set.

I’d like to clarify an edge case around what it means for *“all containers to have limits set”*.

Consider a pod with three containers:

* Container A sets a CPU limit but does **not** set a memory limit
* Container B sets a memory limit but does **not** set a CPU limit
* Container C sets both CPU and memory limits

In this situation, each resource dimension (CPU, memory) is covered by at least one container, but **no single container defines limits for all resources**.

My questions are:

* Should this pod be treated as *not having all container limits set*, and therefore **skip defaulting pod-level limits and return early**?
* Or should defaulting be evaluated **per resource dimension**, meaning we aggregate CPU limits from containers that define CPU limits and memory limits from containers that define memory limits?
* If the latter is intended, how should we treat containers that omit a specific resource limit — should they be assumed unbounded for that resource, or excluded from the aggregation?

I want to ensure the implementation aligns with the intent behind avoiding pods having access to “unknown” resources while still handling partial container specifications consistently.

Any clarification or pointers to prior discussions would be very helpful.

Looking at nginx Ingress, here is the information gather by my 'agent'...

Short answer: the controller does not special‑case, normalize, or reject IP addresses in the Ingress rule hosts. It passes the string through and renders it into NGINX’s server_name as-is. That has different outcomes for IPv4 vs IPv6.

What happens in code
- Host is taken verbatim into the Server object
  - controller.createServers(): rule.Host is copied into server.Hostname (empty -> "_") with no IP/DNS validation
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/controller.go
- The NGINX template renders server_name using that hostname unchanged (except for wildcard handling)
  - template: server_name {{ buildServerName $server.Hostname }} …
    - file: rootfs/etc/nginx/template/nginx.tmpl
  - buildServerName only rewrites wildcard names; otherwise returns the input string
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/template/template.go (buildServerName)
- Admission/safety checks do not reject IP hosts
  - inspector.CheckRegex() only blocks dangerous substrings (alias/root/etc); it does not validate DNS vs IP
    - file: internal/ingress/inspector/{ingress.go,rules.go}
- TLS certificate selection for such a host will use the host string
  - verifyHostname() treats IPs specially and only matches against IP SANs
    - file: internal/ingress/controller/certificate.go (verifyHostname)

Resulting behavior
- IPv4 host (e.g., 203.0.113.10)
  - NGINX gets: server_name 203.0.113.10; This is valid in NGINX and will match requests whose Host header is that IP.
  - TLS: the controller will associate a cert only if it has the IP in its SANs; otherwise it falls back to the default cert. Note many clients don’t send SNI for IP literals, so the default cert may be served at handshake time regardless.
- IPv6 host (e.g., 2001:db8::1)
  - NGINX would be rendered with: server_name 2001:db8::1; Colons aren’t valid in server_name tokens. On reload, the controller runs nginx -t (testTemplate in internal/ingress/controller/nginx.go); nginx -t will fail, so the reload is aborted and the previous (last good) config stays active.

Bottom line
- The controller accepts and forwards IP hosts unchanged.
- IPv4 literal hosts work (host-based vhost keyed to the IP in the Host header); TLS requires an IP SAN to avoid cert mismatch. 
- IPv6 literal hosts cause an invalid NGINX configuration and prevent reload.

Note: Per Kubernetes networking.k8s.io/v1 spec, Ingress .spec.rules[].host is a DNS name. Most clusters will reject IPs at API validation, so you typically can’t create such Ingresses. The above describes what the controller does if it nevertheless receives one (e.g., older API/validation gap).
IPv6 is not a valid 'domain name' anyway though, so it would still not pass the domain name validation, and just not be supported.

Here is the info about the Gateway behavior: in short, the IP V4 would get through, but is not supposed to be supported.
I will test behavior with Envoy Gateway provider as a started and see what happens, but Gateway may also need some formal modification to support this fully.

> Short answer:
> - Not supported. Gateway API Hostname fields explicitly disallow IP literals. That applies to both IPv4 and IPv6.
> - IPv6 literals will be rejected by schema validation (fail fast at admission) because the Hostname regex only allows DNS labels (no colons/brackets).
> - IPv4 literals are also disallowed by spec; however, the regex used for Hostname matches RFC1123 labels and can accept something that looks like 10.0.0.1. Although such values may be admitted by the API server, they are non-conformant and behavior is implementation-specific. Do not rely on them.
> 
> What the code and CRDs say:
> - apis/v1/shared_types.go: Hostname string
>   • Comment: “IPs are not allowed.”
>   • Validation: Pattern ^(\*\.)?[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*$
> - apis/v1/httproute_types.go (and grpc/tls routes): Hostname/hostnames fields repeat “IPs are not allowed.”
> - Listener.hostname is also Hostname (same regex and rule; config/crd/.../gateways.yaml has XValidations using the same pattern). 
> - TLSRoute SNI hostnames: CRD descriptions explicitly state “IPs are not allowed in SNI names per RFC 6066.”
> - PreciseHostname (used e.g., for HTTPRequestRedirect.hostname and some response rewriting): comment says numeric IP addresses are not allowed with its own pattern.
> 
> Expected behavior by case:
> - HTTPRoute.spec.hostnames or GRPCRoute.spec.hostnames set to an IPv6 literal (e.g., [2001:db8::1], or 2001:db8::1): rejected at admission with a pattern-validation error. This is a graceful, early failure.
> - Listener.hostname set to IPv6 literal: same, rejected at admission.
> - Any field typed as PreciseHostname set to IP (v4 or v6): rejected at admission.
> - HTTPRoute/GRPCRoute hostnames set to IPv4 literal (e.g., 10.0.0.1): spec says “IPs are not allowed”, but the regex can admit this because RFC1123 permits numeric labels. If admitted, it’s non-conformant; controllers are not required to support it. Possible outcomes are implementation-specific: some may ignore/mismatch; others may match literally; status conditions like NoMatchingListenerHostname could appear depending on the controller’s handling. There is no guarantee.
> 
> Guidance and workarounds:
> - Don’t use IPs in Hostname/hostnames anywhere in Gateway API routing rules. Use DNS names.
> - If you need to accept requests addressed to the Gateway IP (client sends Host: 10.0.0.1), leave Listener.hostname and Route hostnames unset so they match all hostnames; route by path/headers instead. You cannot explicitly match the IP literal via hostnames in a conformant way.
> - For fields that describe external origins/URIs (e.g., CORSOrigin, AbsoluteURI), IP hosts are allowed, but those are not used for hostname routing intersection; they are separate features.
> 
> Bottom line:
> - IPv4 and IPv6 IPs are not supported as Gateway routing hostnames. IPv6 is always rejected by schema; IPv4 may pass schema but is still out-of-spec and behavior is controller-dependent. Prefer DNS names or leave hostnames empty to match all.

Hmm, this still shows at least a concurrency issue in our tests that could be triggered. I think that warrants a fix at minimum. 

> Without this artificial delay, the initialization completes before any other code can interact with the locks.

Are we sure about this? While it seems unlikely that this can happen, I looked through the traces and spotted some concerning sections with the sleep that @user12031 showed.

The run lock is trying to be acquired by the `run` function and the distribute function is being called by `processReplacedListInfo` in `controller.go`. This does seem like it can happen in a real scenario, however unlikely it is.

```
	defer wg.Wait()                                         // Wait for Processor to stop
	defer stopProcessor(errors.New("informer is stopping")) // Tell Processor to stop
	// TODO: extend the MutationDetector interface so that it optionally
	// has a RunWithContext method that we can use here.
	wg.StartWithChannel(processorStopCtx.Done(), s.cacheMutationDetector.Run)
	wg.StartWithContext(processorStopCtx, s.processor.run)

	defer func() {
		s.startedLock.Lock()
		defer s.startedLock.Unlock()
		s.stopped = true // Don't want any new listeners
	}()
	s.controller.RunWithContext(ctx)
```

Due to the fact that wg.Wait only pauses after `s.controller.RunWithContext(ctx)` starts up is a bit of a concern. This seems like the root cause of the issue, since the controller will eventually trigger a replace which adds elements to the informer before it is started, strange...

Since this hasn't been reported on a live env, it seems likely that the informer starts up far quicker than the controller starts pushing events, but I agree that this looks like a real deadlock, possibly worse than just a goroutine leak. I think the main reason we don't see this is that the controller starting a watch is a far greater magnitude of time than the startup time of an informer.

  Goroutine 24 - User: ./staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/mux.go:268 k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch.(*Broadcaster).loop (0xb0207f) [chan receive]
  Goroutine 25 - User: ./staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go:1024 k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache.(*processorListener).add (0xfb2549) [chan send]
  Goroutine 27 - User: /nvme/gopath/go-1.25.2/src/runtime/sema.go:100 sync.runtime_SemacquireRWMutexR (0x48be05) [wait for GC cycle]
  Goroutine 28 - User: /nvme/gopath/go-1.25.2/src/sync/mutex.go:46 sync.(*Mutex).Lock (0x4a233f) [trace reader (blocked)]
  Goroutine 29 - User: /nvme/gopath/go-1.25.2/src/runtime/sema.go:114 sync.runtime_SemacquireWaitGroup (0x48bece) [preempted]
* Goroutine 32 - User: /nvme/gopath/go-1.25.2/src/runtime/sema.go:105 sync.runtime_SemacquireRWMutex (0x48be65) [GC worker (idle)]
```

- 32 in sharedProcessor.shouldResync tries to lock `p.listenersLock`, called by `startResync`
- 29 in watchWithResync waits for 32 to stop
- 28 in RealFIFO.Close tries to lock f.lock
- 27 in sharedProcessor.run tries to lock p.listenersLock before starting the listeners (this is what got delayed)
- 25 in processorListener.add tries to write to p.addCh
- 24 in Broadcaster.loop tries to read m.incoming

So who holds `p.listenersLock`? It's goroutine 25, holding the lock in sharedProcessor.distribute while being blocked during event delivery.

So it seems the problem is that sharedProcessor.distribute assumes that sharedProcessor.run has started all listeners, but prevents that from happening when reached to soon.

I wonder whether `sharedProcessor.distribute` should check that all listeners have been started. If not, yield the mutex and wait on a condition. Code starting the listeners must signal that mutex.

Yep, my thought as well. Let me see if there's an easy way to handle this from distribute. Otherwise, we may have to wait to call `s.controller.RunWithContext(ctx)` until the listeners are started inside of the run function.
Perhaps tracking "started" for each listener is overkill. The global `p.listenersStarted` might be good enough because `sharedProcessor.addListener` will not block while holding the mutex.

some musings:
first and foremost, this small enhancement seems reasonnable and useful to me. I agree it would be good to have it.

next, I'd also prefer kubelet to set the values because the current model is kubelet owning the node and the cgroup management of pods (with everything else built upon that).
I'm advocating since quite some time to start thinking about how the kubelet can delegate these responsabilities to other components, like a [CPU DRA driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-cpu), so why prefer kubelet owning this setting? Because I think the best path is for the community to agree and design a proper delegation model rather than go piecewise following specific issues, because this creates a fragmented space harder to integrate later on and an explosion of special conditions, which we have plenty already. The path should be _conceptually_ like docker -> CRI we did in the quite distant past (and we can totally start with a small well defined core and iterate later on).

So, kubelet should own it only if the kernel supports it, which seems fair so far. Next question would be if use should control it or not (e.g. emergency disable). I think defaulting to this behavior seems the most user-friendly choice and an emergency disable FG seems the best approach.

Which made me think if this work deserves a small KEP because we're actually doing all the things the KEP process mandates, but informally here: thinking about integration parts, impacts on the ecosystem, UX flow, failure modes...

1. Expected positive impact (design objective)

a:cpu.idle, Permission problem or the cgroup controller is not attached: log error, BestEffort cgroup configuration failure
The more difficult problem is:

@ffromani Hi， I saw this PR today. According to your question, I have a deep look at the code, and I answer your question. There may be some mistakes, which can be corrected:
1. According to the code tracking, the main concurrency sources in the call tree of kubelet are:
A: Pod Scope Administration of Topology Manager (serial but different pods can be concurrent)
Call chain:
TopologyManager.Admit() -> calculateAffinity() -> allocateAlignedResources() -> provider.Allocate(pod, container)  ->DeviceManager.Allocate() 
All containers of a single pod call allocateAlignedResources serially. However, different pods can enter the administration process concurrently. There is no global lock to protect the Allocate calls between different pods
B: Reallocation in SyncPod process (concurrent with administration)

There are multiple issues here, lets split them:

1) On gang scheduling semantics for LWS vs Deployment. The Workload api doesn't specify how gang scheduling is applied to a specific "deployment" api (LWS, Deployment, StatefulSet etc.), it is more about how one sets the selectors. If one sets the selectors to define a gang as pods in a Deployment, then that Deployment's pods will be gang scheduled. For cases like LWS, which defines groups of pods as replicas, then the workload api also gives the ability to define "replicated gangs". So I don't believe there is inconsistency.

2) On minCount, this is specific to gang scheduling of pods (pods specifically, not "replicas", as in not LWS replicas, only pods within the gang) that should be scheduled in an all-or-nothing manner. Management of individual replicas, whether the replica is a group of pods (in LWS case) or individual pods (in Deployment case), is a separate matter from gang scheduling. 

3) On minCount and the lack of guarantees for the leader, I indeed think this is a gap, but it should be possible to amend the api 
to take this case into account. Great catch!

4) On managing groups of replicas (for example at least x prefill and y decode), whether a replica is a pod or a group of pods, this is not looked at as a gang-scheduling (all-or-nothing) problem per se; k8s has an API called PodDisruptionBudget (PDB), admittedly the name is legacy and is focused on Pods, but there is an effort to change that to give it "Replica Disruption Budget" semantics so that we can apply the concept on application apis like LWS. However, as you mention in the second gap, I agree that we should revisit this and discuss if scheduling policies across replicas is a concept that we want to bring to the new Workload api, keep it in PDB or propose a third api.   

  The current gang-scheduling capability in the workload api (which again is pod-centric) covers some of this for the single-node case only because for single-node a replica is a pod, not because it is intentionally trying to support it for single-node and not for multi-node.

Just to summarize my thoughts, I am aligned on addressing the two gaps, specifically: 

1) Allow specifying that the leader in a gang is a must to schedule even when a minCount is set
2) Defining inter-replica scheduling policies, whether by expanding the workload api to capture those policies or via PDB

I agree that this should ultimately be addressed by a gang-of-gangs abstraction, but I am concerned that an initial implementation may not fully meet the requirements. A natural first approach to gang-of-gangs is to treat each component (e.g., prefill-leader, prefill-worker, decode-leader, decode-worker) as contributing to a single top-level gang with a set of aggregate minCount constraints (for example, at least one prefill leader and one group of three prefill workers), while still maintaining the existing per-component minCount semantics (e.g., prefill workers scheduled in groups of three).

While this model is sufficient for initial placement, it becomes limiting once scaling is introduced. In particular, it does not provide a clear way to express which components must be gang-scheduled together versus which can scale independently. For example, when scaling both prefill and decode, we typically want prefill leaders and prefill workers to be scheduled as a unit, without being blocked by an inability to schedule additional decode leaders. A flat top-level gang constraint risks coupling unrelated components during scaling, leading to unnecessary scheduling stalls.

 Aside: The difficulties of concisely and clearly encoding these types of constraints while retaining familiar k8s workflows like scaling and rolling updates into resources like Deployment or LeaderWorkerSet are why we built Grove, but Grove is fundamentally still an intent-layer. To be able to provide the full functionality using default kube-scheduler it would need Workload API to support richer semantics around gang-scheduling and eventually topology aware scheduling.

I talked to a kernel nftables hacker (Florian) and he confirmed that this is the "check that there are no loops" code. (When adding new rules or verdict map elements, it needs to confirm that all `jump`s/`goto`s only go to chains you haven't hit yet, so there can't be loops.) Coincidentally, he was actually just working on this code (https://lore.kernel.org/netfilter-devel/20251126114703.8826-1-fw@strlen.de/) and said he'll send a slightly improved version of that patch soon. But he also confirmed there's no way to fix this with existing kernels other than "have fewer jumps/chains".

We had talked before about squashing the endpoint chains into the service chains; instead of doing

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  numgen random mod 2 vmap {
    0 : goto endpoint-UNZV3OEC-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80__10.180.0.4/80 ,
    1 : goto endpoint-5RFCDDV7-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80__10.180.0.5/80
  }
```

it would just do

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  numgen random mod 2 vmap {
    0 : meta l4proto tcp dnat to 10.180.0.4:80 ,
    1 : meta l4proto tcp dnat to 10.180.0.5:80
  }
```

The problem with this is that the endpoint chain doesn't _just_ do DNAT; it also does masquerade-if-hairpin and, potentially, affinity. Affinity is sort of complicated, but it doesn't apply to most services, so we could just ignore that for now ("ignore" = "don't change the rule structure for services using affinity"). So, given that, if we could redo the hairpin handling to not need endpoint-specific rules, then we could get rid of the endpoint chains in _most_ cases. And I guess we could do that with a post-dnat dummy map:

```
add rule ip kube-proxy service-LAUZTJTB-ns4/svc4/tcp/p80
  ip saddr . ip daddr vmap {
    10.180.0.4 . 10.180.0.4 : jump mark-for-masquerade ,
    10.180.0.5 . 10.180.0.5 : jump mark-for-masquerade
  }
```

I guess it would be better if we eliminated the `jump` here too. `mark-for-masquerade` just does `mark set mark or 0x4000`, but we can't put that into a vmap.... I guess we could just squash all of the hairpin handling into a single map lookup in `services` rather than having per-service hairpin handling...

On the `nft` issues, this is a topic Dan and I commented several times, should we use `nft` userspace or should we use `netlink` interface directly?

The main tradeoff is complexity to gain performance and also to reduce userspace dependencies (you can use distroless images so security fixes and image updates are only related to golang)

I started moving some of the projects completely to the netlink format and also documented the process in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kindnet/blob/main/docs/nftables-netlink.md

- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kube-network-policies/pull/136
- https://github.com/aojea/kindnet/pull/139

As you can see, is way simpler to use Dan's library https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/knftables , but at the cost of shelling out and having to delegate to `nft` all the preprocessing. On the contrary, we need to implement all the preprocessing in golang to generate the corresponding bytecode ...

I think that if we are targeting this scale, we can open a KEP to move kube-proxy nftables to netlink , so we can remove one of the bottlenecks that is `nft`

Note that switching to netlink would not help with the kernel side of this bug, which is solely about how many chains and jumps you have, not about how you create them.

However, it would likely help with the "nft using lots of CPU" part (which is unrelated to the kernel softlock).

> I guess we could just squash all of the hairpin handling into a single map lookup in `services` rather than having per-service hairpin handling...

(of course if we switch to raw netlink then we don't even need a map; the nftables bytecode lets you write a rule that does "if source IP equals dest IP", there's just no way to express that in the high-level nftables language.)

## Summary of Windows Volume Resolution Refactor

### Key Improvements

1. **Universal Volume Resolution**  
   The logic no longer relies on fragile drive-letter assumptions (`X:\`). It now uses PowerShell’s `(Get-Item -Path ...).Target` to resolve the actual underlying volume for:
   - Drive letters  
   - NTFS directory mounts  
   - Symlinks  

2. **CSI Proxy Alignment**  
   Volume size retrieval now mirrors the CSI Proxy’s robust approach, using branching logic to correctly handle both simple drive letters and complex Volume GUIDs.

3. **Accurate Size Retrieval**  
   For GUID-based volumes, the function now follows the correct resolution chain:

As part of the Workload Aware Scheduling we are trying to solve the problem with node autoscaling in the scheduler core, but also more generic problem of node scale ups including the GPU device attachment.

The main mechanism that we're thinking of relies on
1. Advertising _Potential Resources_,
1. Reserving _Potential Resources_, them and turning into _Upcoming Resources_
1. Having an ability to allocate not-existing-yet _Upcoming Resources_ and
1. Waiting until they get provisioned (created) as _Actual Resources_.

We believe that waiting for resources should not be a part of the binding process but handled independently earlier, but since we don't have it yet, modeling it as binding conditions sounds like a reasonable approach for now.

So, it should be possible to do exactly the same thing here and allocate not-existing-yet _Upcoming Device_ (predict `DeviceRequestAllocationResult`) before it gets attached and before it is offered in a `ResourceSlice`? When the predicted device appears in a `ResourceSlice`, it would be already "allocated", so it could not be taken by any other Pod.

If that was possible, we could replace the proposed taint mechanism in the First Step (which has some drawbacks). I'm less certain how to properly model the second step and AFAIK we don't have any concrete proposal for the autoscaling part either (@44past4 and @x13n are looking into this part), but I'd imagine it as follows:

The fabric devices are offered as two different sets of devices
1. Fake _Potential Devices_ used for scheduling that are later replaced with predicted node-local _Upcoming Devices_
2. _Reservation Devices_ controlling the attachment process and keeping track how many fabric devices are available and outlives fake + node-local allocation

The flow would be the following
1. The fabric device are offered as described here (same `driverName` and GPU model) as _Potential Devices_
2. When scheduler picks one of those devices, allocator will do:
2a. Create new ResourceClaim to acquire a _Reservation Device_ (similar to the Extended Devices design)
2b. Allocation of the _Reservation Device_ decrements a counter of available _Potential Devices_ for scheduling
2c. Allocate predicted (not-existing-yet) node-local device (_Upcoming Device_) and set binding conditions blocking the binding
2d. The physical attachment process starts and holds the process until the attachment is complete (the _Upcoming Device_ becomes _Actual Device_)
3. When the attachment is complete, pod can be bound holding both the _Reservation Device_ and _Actual Device_

There's another approach that was discussed earlier: wrap the vendor DRA driver on the node. The wrapper sits between the DRA driver and kubelet and between the DRA driver and the apiserver. Initially, the DRA driver sees only local devices. The wrapper let's it publish those. Devices shared between nodes are published by the control plane, using a different pool ID and the same DRA driver name.

Now when one of those devices is allocated, pod scheduling triggers binding:
- The device gets attached to the node.
- The vendor DRA driver is restarted, seeing a new device and trying to publish it.
- The wrapper filters out that new device, so it's never visible to the scheduler and thus cannot be taken for another pod.
- The wrapper intercepts the NodePrepare/Unprepare calls, replacing the "pool ID" such that the vendor DRA driver thinks it is dealing with its own, "local" device.

Detaching the device reverts this.

With this approach, no further changes are necessary in the control plane. ResourceSlices don't need to be rewritten. It is more work "downstream" because this wrapper needs to be implemented.

@johnbelamaric, @pohly, @dom4ha ## Summary of the Proposal To enable the happy path for BindingConditions, I would like to propose the following two mechanisms: 1. A mechanism to replace a device that was already allocated in the AllocationResult while the scheduler is waiting for BindingConditions in the PreBind phase, with another device from a different `ResourceSlice` (specified via a newly introduced `ReservedDeviceID` field). 2. To prevent device stealing during the above replacement, we introduce the unique identifier(`GlobalID`) per-device as optional parameter in ResourceSlice, and this identifier is used to link devices across different ResourceSlice objects. Details on how to implement these mechanisms are described in the following sections. ## Background To realize dynamic attachment of fabric devices (e.g., CXL devices) to nodes—particularly as an extension of the BindingConditions happy path in DRA—the “replacement” mechanism described above is essential. This is because, in general, the vendor managing the fabric and the vendor providing the device (e.g., NVIDIA) are different entities. When exposing these devices to DRA via `ResourceSlice`, the expected responsibility split is: - When the device exists in the fabric (i.e., not attached to any node): the fabric vendor’s driver should output the information. - When the device is already attached to a node: the device vendor should output the information. Assuming that the source of `ResourceSlice` differs before and after attachment, we need a replacement mechanism to achieve the following happy-path sequence: 1. Reserve the pre-attach state device for the Pod. 2. Attach the device to a node, then schedule/deploy the Pod onto that node and let it use the device. If the fabric vendor and the device vendor were the same, a single `ResourceSlice` might suffice to represent both states. However, this is not realistic in practice. A previously suggested proxy pattern on the kubelet-plugin side (with the fabric vendor acting as a proxy) is also problematic: standardizing interfaces between fabric vendors and device vendors is difficult (Kubernetes cannot enforce such standards), and would require bilateral coordination between each fabric vendor and each device vendor—making real-world adoption unlikely. ## Implementation Caveats There are several important points to consider when implementing the replacement mechanism: 1. No inconsistencies must be introduced by replacement. At no point in time should a device from the same `ResourceSlice` be assigned to multiple `ResourceClaim` `AllocationResult`s. This requires careful consideration of the Scheduler’s internal caches, etc. Since the Scheduler owns those caches, replacement must be performed by the Scheduler (and only there). 2. We need a mechanism to prevent device stealing for the device targeted for replacement. Here, “stealing” means: one Pod triggers the fabric device attachment, but before it actually acquires the now-attached device via the replacement mechanism, another Pod grabs that node-attached device. If we attempted to prevent stealing strictly using existing capabilities, it might be possible with very complex controls in an external controller (e.g., sophisticated use of Taints or access control at the device-driver layer). However, there is no simple, scheduler-only guarantee against stealing today. As long as the first caveat (no inconsistency) is satisfied, stealing itself is not fatal (we could opt to tolerate stealing, or rely on an external controller to prevent it). Therefore, anti-stealing is not strictly required. That said, it would be desirable to offer an optional, scheduler-level mechanism to reduce or prevent stealing. ## Concrete Design ### 1. Mechanism for Replacement Add the following field to `ResourceClaim`: - **`ReservedDeviceID`** In practice, this field is expected to hold a triple used by DRA to identify a device: driver name, pool name, and device name. When we want to perform replacement, an external controller fills the new `ReservedDeviceID` field of the `ResourceClaim` with the target DeviceID for replacement, and then sets the BindingConditions to true. When the Scheduler observes that the BindingConditions are satisfied, it checks whether the device specified by `ReservedDeviceID` is not used elsewhere (carefully, to avoid conflicts), and then overwrites the existing `AllocationResult` within the happy path (PreBind). ### 2. Mechanism to Prevent Stealing Introduce an optional new field called `GlobalID` in `ResourceSlice`. This is a per-device unique identifier (string), typically something like a UUID. In the original DRA model, a device was uniquely identified by `DeviceID` (the triple: driver name, pool name, device name). In the new mechanism, we define that devices with the same `GlobalID` are considered the same physical device, even if their driver name or pool name differ. For the happy path of dynamically attaching/detaching fabric devices: - The fabric vendor’s `ResourceSlice` (1), and - The device vendor’s `ResourceSlice` (2) should both set the same `GlobalID`. If (1) is already allocated in an `AllocationResult`, then any device in (2) with the same `GlobalID` must be protected from being allocated to other Pods. This provides an anti-stealing safeguard. Because this field did not exist before, device vendors will need to populate `GlobalID` in their drivers. However, we believe this does not impose a heavy implementation burden. ## Notes on the Anti-Stealing Measure The above anti-stealing mechanism only works when the individual device identity is discernible while the device is still in the fabric. In practice, this is not always guaranteed. For example, a fabric might hide per-device identity while the device is in the fabric and only expose model/count-level information; individual identity may become known only after the device is attached to a node. In such cases, the `GlobalID`-based anti-stealing mechanism cannot be used. Therefore, specifying `GlobalID` should remain strictly optional. If `GlobalID` is not used, the Scheduler does not assume responsibility for preventing stealing—users can either rely on external controllers to mitigate stealing or accept the possibility of stealing as part of their operational model. ## Relation to WAS and Short‑Term Improvements @dom4ha has emphasized the idea of using WAS (such as potential node/device evaluation), but this approach is fundamentally a long‑term improvement. It requires new abstractions, additional coordination with drivers, and broader architectural changes across the scheduler. More importantly, even with WAS, devices may still transition from “potential → actual” due to changes in device/node state. This means the scheduler will still need a mechanism to prevent unnecessary re-scheduling. Therefore, regardless of whether WAS is adopted later, we need a common short‑term mechanism that: - prevents re-scheduling, - handles potential -> actual transitions safely, This solution remains necessary even in the presence of WAS and should be included as the foundational behavior of the scheduler.

Different entities writing the same field sounds a bit suspicious to me. But let's see where exactly that field is.

> Introduce an optional new field called GlobalID in ResourceSlice. This is a per-device unique identifier (string), typically something like a UUID. [...] The fabric vendor’s ResourceSlice (1), and The device vendor’s ResourceSlice (2) should both set the same GlobalID.

How are controller and vendor supposed to determine this GlobalID so that it is the same? That seems to have the same problem as the proxy approach (need tight coordination between both parties).

That aside, I can see how this approach to "anti-stealing" would work. I'm a bit wary of the complexity of the implementation, but at least conceptually it seems okay. I agree that it can be optional.

> Add where?

Found it in the diagram: it's in `DeviceRequestAllocationResult`.

I don't see a need for the scheduler to set `ReservedDeviceID` there: the device is already "reserved" because it is allocated. The scheduler also wouldn't know when to set and when not to set `ReservedDeviceID`.

We can allow the controller to set a `ReplaceWith` field in `DeviceRequestAllocationResult` together with setting the binding condition. That's an atomic update, so we have no concurrency problems. Then when the scheduler next tries pod scheduling, it can take `ReplaceWith` into account:
- If that device is available, update the allocation and proceed.
- If that device is not available, deallocate the claim and try again.

This puts a lot of trust into the controller. It must make sure that the device it replaces with satisfies the requests. We may want to double-check that in the scheduler, to catch mistakes.

> Add where?

In the diagram above, ReservedDeviceID is listed within AllocationResult, but it should be included in the AllocatedDeviceStatus field.

Our understanding is that the controller performs the device attachment process. After the attached device is finalized, the controller writes the ReservedDeviceID into AllocatedDeviceStatus. Subsequently, the controller sets BindingConditions to True.

The scheduler, after BindingConditions are satisfied, replaces the DeviceID in the AllocationResult with the ReservedDeviceID information if the ReservedDeviceID exists, the corresponding resource actually exists in the vendor's ResourceSlice, and it is not already allocated to another ResourceClaim.

> How are controller and vendor supposed to determine this GlobalID so that it is the same? That seems to have the same problem as the proxy approach (need tight coordination between both parties).

For example, the GPU's UUID. This is a globally unique identifier recorded in the hardware's registers.

If a vendor's DRA implements registering such UUIDs to a GlobalID, the fabric controller can register the same GlobalID to its own fabric ResourceSlice according to that UUID's format.
(That is, it depends on the vendor DRA implementation.)

> Add where?

The position of `ReservedDeviceID` shown in the diagram was incorrect.
It is actually located in `AllocatedDeviceStatus`, and it is intended to be set by the controller, not by the scheduler.

Therefore, I believe this approach is close to your `ReplaceWith` proposal.
The only difference is that they are added to different structures:
`ReplaceWith` ⊂ `DeviceRequestAllocationResult`, whereas `ReservedDeviceID` ⊂ `AllocatedDeviceStatus`.

> Different entities writing the same field sounds a bit suspicious to me.

By having the controller set into `AllocatedDeviceStatus`, we can address the concern you mentioned—
that different entities would write to the same field.
This also avoids inconsistencies with the scheduler’s internal cache.

**GlobalID**

- `DeviceRequestAllocationResult`
- `Device` (`ResourceSlice.spec.devices`)

**ReservedDeviceID**

- `AllocatedDeviceStatus`

Is this a matter of design philosophy - i.e., not wanting to perform scheduling work such as allocation within the binding cycle -

> Is this a matter of design philosophy - i.e., not wanting to perform scheduling work such as allocation within the binding cycle - or is it fundamentally impossible to implement in the first place?

The scheduling phase is there to guarantee cache consistency and binding is by design async, so it's rather a design philosophy.

The PostFilter extension point is more suitable for handling cases where initial placement is not feasible. This phase is supposed to come up with alternatives (for instance do some preemption) and device attachment theoretically fits into this model. Everything happens within scheduling cycle and pods don't go to binding until resources become available (pod got preempted).

The problem is that we want to "advertise" attachable devices as if they were already available, so we don't reach PostFilter phase. Scheduling over potential resources is definitely something we want to support in WAS (integrate scaling with scheduling), but it's hard to do it quickly short term.

We can think about short therm alternatives, but nothing obvious works and it's hard to dedicate time considering the current load priorities we have.

In my head, there's these patterns: 
1. custom-pluginA -> DRA -> custom-pluginB -> volume binding.
2. custom-pluginA -> DRA -> volume binding -> custom-pluginB.

We need to decide what to do when one plugin disables parallel execution. Should we run all PreBind plugins sequentially, or should we try to get best effort parallelism if multiple plugins suitable for parallel execution are set one after another? The first solution seems safer, but the second looks like a good optimization. However, I don't think it would cause any problems.

I imagined the second option on your comment. 
So, the point is, when custom-pluginA -> DRA -> volume binding -> custom-pluginB (while custom plugins have `allowParallel: false`), whether users expect DRA and volume binding to also run one after another, or they are ok to run them in parallel as long as their custom plugins are running before/after DRA and volume binding.  ...and, I can only imagine the second case, not the first case.

One more thing that's in my mind - imagine we have a following sequence of PreBind plugins specified in the configuration:

```
DynamicResources -> VolumeBinding -> CustomPluginA -> CustomPluginB

and the ones that have `allowParallel` set to true are `DynamicResources`, `VolumeBinding` and `CustomPluginB`.

Let's say that for a particular Pod in the binding cycle, we skip only `CustomPluginA`.

Are we ok with running all three plugins in parallel or should we run `DynamicResources` and `VolumeBinding` in parallel - and only after their (successful) completion, kick off `CustomPluginB`?

Of course, it all boils down to the semantics of the `allowParallel` we define in here - but if I were to guess, it'd be "safer" (from breaking-change-o-logy's POV) to follow the latter approach.

This is an unfortunate problem.

The history:

Once upon a time, we did not do anything special with the `clusterIP` field.  People would `kubectl create` a service, get assigned a `clusterIP`, then `kubectl replace` the same input (maybe modified labels) and apiserver would fail because it detected the user trying to UNSET the `clusterIP`.  Weird - they didn't set the field in the first place, why should they need to specify it in the replace?

It seems reasonable that it should be idempotent. 

So we added support to quietly carry-forward the old clusterIP if it is not set in the new object.

It seems that you *actually* want to unset the `clusterIP`, but now you CAN'T, because our super smart implementation turns it into a silent variation of "patch".

Our options, I think, are:

1) Don't carry forward "NONE", since it would never have been auto-assigned (unlike an IP value).
2) Close this as "working as intended".

Changing the behavior could break someone who depends on this behavior.  It is (IMO) _unlikely_ but it is not impossible.

The workaround is to change `type: ExternalName` (and set `externalName: example.com`) in one operation, and then set it back to `type: ClusterIP`, which will trigger the allocation.

Or simply delete the service and recreate it in the new mode.

My preference is the latter -- you work around it.  This is not something that has come up, basically ever.

Clarifying the above comment: 

- `CategorizeEndpoints` decides "which endpoint IPs kube-proxy should forward packets to"
- `addEndpoints` (which we are modifying here) tries to figure out "which `discoveryv1.Endpoint` corresponds to the Pod that is *actually* receiving traffic for `endpointIP`". The answer to that question might be an Endpoint that we want to forward traffic to, or it might be an Endpoint that we *don't* want to forward traffic to, but we're not deciding that here. We just need to pick the correct `Endpoint` here so that `CategorizeEndpoints` can make the correct decision later.

Consider two clusters: in both clusters, Service X is `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` and has three Endpoints:
- Endpoint A, with IP `10.128.0.2` which is local and ready
- Endpoint B, with IP `10.128.0.2` which is remote and serving-terminating
- Endpoint C, with IP `10.130.0.5` which is local and serving-terminating

However:
- In Cluster 1, Endpoint B is fake/wrong. Traffic sent to `10.128.0.2` will always be forwarded to Endpoint A.
- In Cluster 2, Endpoint A is fake/wrong. Traffic sent to `10.128.0.2` will always be forwarded to Endpoint B.

If `addEndpoints` prefers local endpoints to non-local endpoints, then it will keep Endpoint A, and discard Endpoint B. Then later, `CategorizeEndpoints` will be asked to consider Endpoint A and Endpoint C, and it would say "well, Endpoint A is local and ready, while Endpoint C is not ready, so we'll keep just Endpoint A" and so it would then send all traffic for Service X to `10.128.0.2`.

In cluster 1, that is the correct outcome. But in cluster 2, that's wrong: `10.128.0.2` *actually* routes to a remote Pod, violating the traffic policy. Kube-proxy *should* have picked Endpoint C instead in cluster 2, but it didn't realize that because `addEndpoints` had kept the wrong duplicate of `10.128.0.2`.

In other words, there is no reason for `addEndpoints` to look at `isLocal` (or `terminating`), because whether an Endpoint is "local" has nothing to do with whether the Endpoint is *real*, which is the thing `addEndpoints` actually needs to know.

And the only rule we've agreed on for deciding which Endpoint is real when there are duplicates is: if one Endpoint is `serving` and the others are not, then the `serving` one is the real one. So `addEndpoints` *should* consider `serving`, but it shouldn't consider the other conditions. (This rule won't help us pick the right Endpoint in the example above, but that's fine, because we have agreed that the example above is a broken cluster and kube-proxy is not expected to be able to figure out the right thing to do there.)

Hm... I was assuming that the existing code was doing the right thing for the "Endpoint gets moved between slices" case, and so we only had to worry about the "two pods have the same IP" case.

But I guess the existing code was slightly off even for the "Endpoint gets moved between slices" case, because it ignored the fact that the Endpoint from the more-recently-written slice would have a more-up-to-date set of `conditions` than the Endpoint from the less-recently-written slice. So if an Endpoint becomes non-`serving` at the same time as it gets moved to a different slice, then in that case we want to prefer the non-`serving` Endpoint in the new slice over the `serving` Endpoint in the old slice, because the non-`serving` one represents the current state.

But... you can't apply the "more-recent slice" rule to the "two pods with the same IP" case: if you have a "ghost" pod stuck in `Terminating` in slice 1, and a real `Ready` pod with the same IP in slice 2, you _always_ want to prefer the Endpoint for the real pod, regardless of which slice was written last.

So, to get both cases right, we have to distinguish whether we're looking at the "temporarily-duplicate Endpoints for a single pod" case or the "persistently-duplicate Endpoints for different pods" case.

So, if two `Endpoint`s have the same `addresses[0]`, then:
- If they have the same `targetRef`, then prefer the one from the more-recently-updated slice.
- If they have different `targetRef`s and only one of them is `serving`, then prefer the one that is `serving`
- Otherwise don't care / undefined.

----

The other thing about this patch is that it relies on kube-proxy perfectly observing all updates as they happen. If kube-proxy gets disconnected and has to resync (or if it starts up while the EndpointSlice controller is in the middle of rewriting a set of slices), it won't always know which slice is the newer one. This could be fixed if the EndpointSlice controller wrote out the sequence numbers to the actual EndpointSlices rather than kube-proxy just trying to compute them itself.

Alternatively, we _could_ just not bother with the "more-recently-updated slice" fix: if we pick the wrong Endpoint, it just means we keep using the older conditions until we receive the other updated slice, which is the same thing that would happen if we had just received the update slightly later. It's not the end of the world, and not even strictly "wrong".

I think you're confusing EndpointSlice event ordering with Pod event ordering.

- Service X has endpoints split across two slices.
- Pod A, with IP "10.0.0.1", starts terminating. Pod A is listed in EndpointSlice 1, so the EndpointSlice controller pushes an update to EndpointSlice 1 with the updated conditions for that Endpoint.
- (Pod A takes a long time to terminate...)
- Pod B starts up and gets assigned IP "10.0.0.1". The EndpointSlice controller decides to stick it in EndpointSlice 2, so it pushes an update to EndpointSlice 2 containing the new Endpoint.
- Pod C starts terminating. Pod C is listed in EndpointSlice 1, so the EndpointSlice controller pushes an update to EndpointSlice 1 with the updated conditions for that Endpoint.

At this point EndpointSlice 1 is newer than EndpointSlice 2, but the information about Pod A in EndpointSlice 1 is _older_ than the information about Pod B in EndpointSlice 2. We have no way of knowing which Endpoint contains newer information in this case, so it doesn't matter which EndpointSlice is newer; we just assume that it's more likely that the running Endpoint represents newer information than the terminating Endpoint.

- Do we need `count` for the first use case? (..most likely Yes). And, how should we design the API for that?
- Is "Basic" the best naming? And, whether should "Basic" be defining the first usecase or the second? Or, should we name it differently?

I've been working on the [Workload API Integration Design](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1oGa_zA1HSlvoAsR-Sks9NBlHe6ytDh5EdxMqmmJNJbE/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.7vj701k0pfja) for how true workload controllers (Job, StatefulSet, LWS, JobSet, etc..) should create and manage Workload objects. This discussion directly impacts that design, so I want to share the controller integration perspective.

If controllers only create Workloads for gang-eligible configurations, we face a dilemma: how do controllers decide when to create Workloads?
- Annotation-based opt-in is fragile and undiscoverable
- Inference from config (e.g., "Parallel policy implies gang") is implicit and potentially surprising. A user might set Parallel for performance reasons without wanting gang semantics. 
- New API field on each workload defeats the purpose of putting `WorkloadRef` on Pod API (avoids changing every workload type)

With `Basic`, controllers can always create Workloads. The only variance is the policy, which maps directly from the workload's configuration:

- StatefulSet Parallel → Gang(minCount=replicas)
- StatefulSet OrderedReady → Basic(desiredCount=replicas)
- Job indexed, parallelism=completions → Gang(minCount=parallelism)
- Job with waves → Basic(desiredCount=parallelism) per wave
- etc ...

In this case, the behavior is uniform and predictable which simplifies controller logic, better UX for the users,  and makes the Workload API discoverable for all workloads, not just gang-eligible ones.

On the count question, I agree with @thockin that `Basic` needs count information to be useful. I had to do make workarounds in the design because this field is not there. Which addresses @wojtek-t's use case "the scheduler can make better placement decisions knowing "100 more pods want the same zone" even without gang constraints".

I've closed https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135085 because reducing resources seems to cause more flakes, which is not what we want. My hypothesis is because lowering requests/limits for each test pod decreases margin for error for the HPA behaviour to actuate.

However, now we have a problem where I believe the existing kube-infra we have is just good "enough" to have serial HPA tests, and I'm not even sure if it can handle concurrency of 2.

The current set up is that we have 3 worker nodes with 2 cores each with a total of 6, (CPU is the bottleneck here). 

Doing some math here (along with help with some AI tools), many tests are [HPA "scale up" tests](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7fbf63a23fcf393d4ba310412155dfbbaa36bb9a/test/e2e/autoscaling/horizontal_pod_autoscaling.go#L238). These run a test consumer deployment with pods with a request/limit of 500m/500MiB. And these can peak at 5 pods, with a total of 2500m or 2.5 cores. That's already over the capacity of one infra node with 1 concurrent test. If we have 2 concurrent tests, we can potentially get to 5 cores at once only using 2 deployments, which is already dangerously close to our total cluster resources of 6 CPU cores.

I tried these tests on an OpenShift cluster where we had 3 worker nodes with 4 cores each for a total of 12 CPU, and this was able to pass with a concurrency of 3 with 1 flake.

@sanposhiho

I’m afraid that increasing the buffer size alone will not solve the problem — at least not completely.
A major part of the issue comes from the fact that each plugin is sampled with a highly uneven probability, and simply modifying the cache size cannot change that.

During the Filter phase, every time a Pod is scheduled, the scheduler performs calculations on N nodes. As long as the cluster is even moderately large, the cache fills up quickly, and subsequent entries get dropped once the buffer is full. As a result, earlier plugins may still get a continuous timeline, while later ones only get a few scattered points, and those near the end may not be observed at all.

To address this, I think there are a few possible approaches:
1.	Instead of only exposing a cache-size parameter, allow users to selectively focus on the plugins they care about.
This way, although the sampling probability remains uneven, users can at least observe the plugins they want, and they will know that missing data is due to not “subscribing” to that metric — rather than being misled by a distorted and intermittent timeline.
I was very puzzled by this graph myself. Before I dug into the cause, the DRA device had already been allocated by the plugin, while the monitoring graph kept showing zero. This was highly misleading.
2.	Introduce an adaptive sampling mechanism that dynamically adjusts the sampling factor.
For example, if the buffer is full, reduce the sampling rate; if it stays underutilized for a long time, gradually increase the sampling rate.
This might give every plugin a more similar probability of being sampled, making the visualization look more sane and consistent.

Or as an quick fix, it might also be possible to extend this patch to allow users to customize the buffer size, and to define a maximum flush rate using something like a token-bucket mechanism.

Finally, may I also ask whether this part has encountered performance issues before?
From my current load tests and understanding, this logic seems to be purely CPU-bound and does not involve any I/O. It also doesn’t appear to become a performance bottleneck. As far as I can tell, Observe simply retrieves the corresponding time series entry from a map and performs a small amount of computation.

> I’m afraid that increasing the buffer size alone will not solve the problem — at least not completely.

Well, increasing the buffer size with configuring higher interval _can_ solve the problem, no? like, you can estimate the high enough values from the average scheduling latency of your scheduler and the cluster size. You can even flush metric values several times within a single scheduling cycle, like your change here would do at a big scale. 

> As long as the cluster is even moderately large, the cache fills up quickly,

Yes, I understand the problem. I mean you can just increase the buffer size to big enough and the interval to be fast enough with your responsibility. I'm not sure why we need to take those fancier/more complex options instead of my simple one.

> Finally, may I also ask whether this part has encountered performance issues before?

This part specifically, no afaik. So, I'm just talking about a possible concern where one goroutine is eating CPU time a lot, and impacting others possibly. You can understand how many times `FlushMetrics` would have to be called even within a single scheduling cycle with this change at a big scale, like what if the cluster size is 5k nodes, or I know there's much bigger clusters in the world. And, given clearly not everyone needs to scrape the metric values always 100% accurately, I don't think it's fare to let everyone invest an additional CPU time for this more frequent metric recording.

Increasing the buffer size and adjusting the flush interval could certainly mitigate the problem, but my point is that this may not be sufficient, rather than that it is infeasible. From a user’s perspective:
	1.	With the current defaults, the monitoring graph is not always accurate and can be misleading, and users are not informed that such limitations exist. Frankly, an incorrect graph can be worse than having no graph at all.
	2.	Introducing two new tuning parameters forces users to reason about “magic numbers” that reflect internal implementation details, and configuring them correctly requires deep background knowledge. > We also hard-coded pluginMetricsSamplePercent and the metrics are not recorded always in the first place. (I'm also fine to expose that parameter as well though)

Hard-coding the sampling rate does not affect correctness, but the issue we’re dealing with is about correctness. An odd or skewed data distribution can be misleading, and this should not happen by default nor require users to manually tweak configurations to fix it.
Moreover, it’s very hard for us to provide any meaningful guidance on what these values should be. We can’t expect users to configure an extremely large buffer or set the flush interval to 0s — that would just push the burden onto them without giving a sensible default.

---
From my perspective, what we really need is a mechanism that keeps the sampling probability across plugins as uniform as possible. Otherwise, plugins that run later in the scheduling cycle become nearly invisible. Increasing the buffer size is one option, but an adaptive sampling strategy — where the sampling rate is reduced when the buffer fills — might provide a more robust solution.

Another possibility is to avoid exposing this metric by default and instead require users to opt in to specific plugins they want to observe, thereby avoiding misleading or skewed visualizations.

Additionally, I want to clarify the original use case in which I relied on this metric: I needed to understand how much latency the DRA plugin introduces into scheduling. This requires that each plugin be sampled with a roughly equal probability. Otherwise, only the first one or two plugins ever show up, and the DRA plugin becomes almost invisible. This creates a highly misleading chart when profiling performance, because it suggests that DRA has no cost when in reality it might simply never be sampled.

> Right, increasing it to an unbounded size would certainly “solve” the problem, but in practice users need to know what a reasonable value is, not an infinite one. And determining that reasonable number is quite difficult, isn’t it?

As I already mentioned, you can roughly estimate the high enough values from the average scheduling latency of your scheduler and the cluster size. Or, just more manually though, you can keep increasing the values until you get enough data points that you need.

> Hard-coding the sampling rate does not affect correctness, but the issue we’re dealing with is about correctness.

It does. It's just that _**you are**_ ok not to collect the metric always. That could also be considered as "correctness" for some other people. like what if users actually need to collect all metric values (`pluginMetricsSamplePercent: 100%`) because e.g., they know some plugins rarely take time for some specific pods, while not for most of others. For them, it might be "incorrect" that the latency p99 doesn't always catch a spike, but today the metric could miss those because we fix the pluginMetricsSamplePercent at 10%. 
Another case, some users may prefer to set `pluginMetricsSamplePercent: 0.1%` without changing the current `interval`/`bufferSize` to mitigate the problem that you mentioned without feeding more CPUs for the metrics reporting. i.e., all plugins' values are likely reported, but smaller scheduling cycles are sampled.

My point is that it's all about the tradeoff between how much resources you're ok to spend for metric reporting vs how perfect you want to make the metric data points to be. And, the best balance between those two _really_ depends on users. That's the reason I prefer to just expose parameters to simply let users decide for now. 

I'm of course open to other options though. If you want to ask my comments for [your initial proposals](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134976#issuecomment-3570735802):
1. I don't dislike it, but we cannot do this soon because the metrics covered by MetricAsyncRecorder are alpha.
2. I do not like it. It would make the reliability of metric values unpredictably unstable, depending on how busy the scheduler is. Like I mentioned, if we silently lower the sampling rate because that would make some spikes less visible in the metric values. People could not trust the metric values at all if p95 is calculated from 1k scheduling cycles vs p99 is calculated from 10 scheduling cycles.

You made a very good point about users potentially needing to increase `pluginMetricsSamplePercent` to 100% in order to observe tail latency (e.g., p99). I hadn’t considered that scenario, and I agree with your reasoning.

That said, and IMHO, about correctness, simply allowing users to tune these parameters may still not be sufficient if we want users to fully trust these metrics. As long as the channel buffer is allowed to drop events on overflow silently, users cannot completely trust the results — even if they set the sampling percent to 100% or the flush interval to 0s.

Moreover, most users cannot accurately determine what a “large enough” buffer is. They may need multiple rounds of trial and error, and without any visibility into whether drops are occurring, they have no way of knowing whether the data they are looking at is valid.

It might be worthwhile to incur some CPU overhead to expose a counter metric for tracking channel overflow events, so that users can reliably detect if this issue occurs, and thereby understand when the metric may be inaccurate and that they may need to adjust the related parameters if they require higher accuracy.

But, note that I'm not saying some people IRL actually _should_ try collecting metrics 100% accurately. Those are all my "extreme" user scenarios, and rather in a real life I'd suggest people (can try but) don't aim to collect metrics 100% _perfectly_. Because you're right: we can _never_ say "this buffer is _always_ large enough for your cluster" since the number of QHint metric records depends on the number of cluster events, which depends on how busy kube-apiserver is. i.e., even if the buffer size is ok enough usually, there could still be some overflow if kube-apiserver is under a unusual busy for some reason. Sorry for my delay, here is my thought and all start with a question:  **Is this metric meaningful when channel overflows are allowed?**

I want to consider the converse: if we allow overflow at this point, are there any usage scenarios where the metric remains useful?

I’m asking because of two reasons:
1.	As you said, this is a trade-off. Collecting this metric has a cost — what do we actually gain?
2.	The answer to (1) determines whether the new params we add whould be a temporary workaround. But, as you also mentioned, we don't want to add a workaround into config, because the current config has reached v1, so once we add something it’s unlikely we’ll be able to remove it later.

Possible valid use cases I can think of
1.	Observe the latency distribution of a specific plugin
	 	Does sampling cause issues? No - With the current implementation’s 20% fixed sampling, the metric is largely usable because the sampling probability is roughly uniform and the sample set as a whole shouldn’t bias the final distribution.
	 	Can overflow cause problems? Yes — overflow could make it impossible to observe that plugin at all, preventing any meaningful observation.
2.	Detect performance spikes in a plugin
		Does sampling cause issues? Yes - As you mentioned earlier, sampling may miss rare long-tail cases; there is room for improvement here, and we will probably need to change the sampling rate to capture those tails.
		Can overflow cause problems? Yes — overflow may drop already-sampled events before they are flushed, so spikes can also be lost.
3.	Other scenarios, I might have missed some—please add anything else you think of.

Conclusion from these scenarios: In the cases I considered, if overflow happens the resulting charts are fundamentally broken — users cannot trust them.

And, How users might consume this chart
1.	Performance-profiling test clusters
This metric is highly detailed and primarily intended for profiling. For profiling, the charts must be as accurate as possible so engineers can know where CPU time is spent. In this scenario, users must carefully tune parameters until overflows stop happening.
2.	Production clusters used by ordinary users
Here users would mainly use the metric as an aid during incident investigation. They pay a small CPU cost and get an imperfect chart. That chart may still miss tails or even hide problematic plugins. Achieving a “perfect” chart may be too expensive for general production use, but fortunately they typically have other metrics to refer to.

IMHO:
1. Under sampling-on conditions, the metric can be useful in some cases. Adding a praram should be fine.
2. But if it allows a large number of overflow events, it becomes effectively useless.  If a user truly needs the metric, they must pay a significant cost preventing it not overflow so to make sure it's reliable. At that point, the control we expose should perhaps be boolean (on/off) rather than a numeric tuning parameter.

  - pros: resource consumption won't change from today. cons: more likely miss the spikes
- Keep the sampling rate, but increase the buffer size/interval
  - pros: catch as many sched cycles as today. cons: more resource.

1.	Even with a larger buffer, the code can still somehow hit the select { default } path eventually.
2.	Since the underlying issue is essentially binary (drop vs. never drop), introducing a numeric parameter may increase cognitive overhead for users without strong justification.

> Although the separate plugin version seems clearer, I'm not sure if this is the right approach. Especially, filtering nodes in PreFilter has some implications (see [#134794 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134794#discussion_r2477057690)) that didn't occur when using NominatedNodeName (or its equivalent code path).

I'm also sceptic about turning this cache into a plugin. Eventually we need to have scheduling logic that works with all plugins and we rather need to aggregate information from all plugins (like the signature) and reason based on it rather than hide the logic inside a plugin. I don't exclude a possibility of having different scheduling logics as different plugins, but I think it's too early to think about it.

I'd make the filtering results cache a part of the framework and the framework would populate it. Also use of PreFilter doesn't seem right as cache results does not consider cluster changes that happen in the meantime, so the results may be both stale and wrong (if node disappeared in the meantime). The way we designed it is to give the suggestion a try, but fallback to the full filtering scan.

Also adding new extension points is more intrusive and visible change to the system as it affects api. We'd need to have a bigger story why it's needed and consider more use cases, so it's something we should have consider during enhancement discussion. Adding it during implementation is more risky.

Overall +1 to what Dominik wrote above. Just emphasizing the 3 most important points from my point of view:

1. I'm definitely against introducing new extension point here. I can't come up with any reasonable usecase for implementing this extension point in a different way, which suggests it's not the best extension point.
Let's not introduce a new API (extension point is effectively a contract of scheduling framework) until we have a very clear usecase for it.

2. I also agree that creating a plugin for it is not really what we want. We know that in 1.36 we will evolve scheduler and introduce a phase that will allow us to process all pods from a workload in a single scheduling cycle (and propose some placement for it). I have very strong intuition that this will be exactly the place where the batching logic will eventually land. So in addition to the argument mentioned above (plugins should be stateless, dependency on plugins, etc.) I just don't think that separate plugin is the target solution.

3. Continuing the above - given that we will most probably be moving that logic around in 1.36, I want this to be as much encapsulated with as few changes to interfaces as possible.

So based on the above, I would actually +1 Dominik's:
"I'd make the filtering results cache a part of the framework and the framework would populate it."

Having gone through the process of adding the plugin now, I am fine with not doing this as a plugin. I was excited that by making it a plugin we would minimize the risk and invasiveness, but it does look like the plugin addition process is both more involved and dangerous than I had hoped. I'll fall back to my original approach with two hook points and a node hint. I am also very much on board with this being part of the framework rather than the scheduler, although the hook points will continue to need to be in the scheduling, obviously. My original proposal remains surprisingly robust. 

I would say (not an issue for today) that the purpose of a framework should be to allow people to add functionality to a pipeline in a way that is both easier and safer than directly modifying the pipeline. I think it is a red flag that it looks safer and lighter-weight to change the core pipeline than add a plugin. And looking at DRA it looks like while it is a plugin, it obviously has deep hooks all over the code, again suggesting the plugin framework isn't working as desired.

TL;DR:

We need the third call to invalidate the cache when a pod comes for another framework or a pod scheduling is aborted after the schedulePod logic concludes. While it makes me nervous not to check, I removed the pod and hint checks; as you said they are not needed, and I remembered that Golang doesn't believe in pre and post conditions, which is not a thing I want to argue at this point. :-) 

I kept a check on the hinted batch. You are correct that we would not currently make the store call because we would exit early, but I really don't want to depend on that subtle connection for correctness. If you feel strongly about it, I would be comfortable with it if we added a comment to the exit condition in schedule_one stating the dependency. That seems more brittle to me, but I can be convinced.

DETAILS:

I would love for us not to need the third call, but I believe we do need it. There are two cases where we need the third call:

 1) When a pod from some other framework gets scheduled we don't have a way to update the cache for this framework. We won't get a call for hint or results, but we will get this completion call. The completion call allows us to clear our state. We have to clear our cache because pods from other frameworks update the node state just like our pods do; the whole point of moving away from the cache approach was to avoid having to reason about the cache when we have interleaved pods coming in.

 2) A pod succeeded in schedulePod, but was then rejected in the subsequent reservation etc code. In this case we can't continue to use the results as if the hint succeeded. This is why we clear when the success bit isn't set. Note that we could have an explicit "failed" call and then avoid the check in the hint code (i.e. keep the logic in the success call), but I feel like it is better this way because we don't have to guarantee we put the failed call on every failure case. Here I could be convinced to go the explicit failure route though; right now it would only be in one spot and it is probably a little easier to follow.

I believe you are correct about not needing to compare the pod across the calls; when called correctly the pod should always match between hint and storage calls, and the hint should always be used if it is given, but I put in the checks to be defensive; I can imagine these things changing (or getting messed up) and would prefer the code to fail "safe". Ideally they should be pre-conditions that are checked in tests, but I realize this is a pattern that go does like. I personally have a strong disagreement with it, but I can have that discussion another time.

> This code change clears up all my confusion. What prompted it, by the way?

Because there exists a race condition between `syncPod` and `doProbe`, the triggering of `syncPod` is not solely initiated by the `proberManager`. When `syncPod` executes `UpdatePodStatus`, the pod may be in one of the following two states:

  * It has not yet been added to the readinessManager. In this case, we directly set the container status to Ready using `ready = !exists`.
  
  * It has been added to the `readinessManager`, but `doProbe` has not yet started execution. In this case, `ready = !exists` evaluates to false, which may cause us to incorrectly set the container status to false.

This serves as a mitigation for the second scenario, ensuring we can escape this race condition.

In container lifecycle code handling, race conditions can potentially occur anywhere, so we must be exceptionally careful. This potential for race conditions is also the reason why we cannot use the `podIsReady` variable derived from the `Conditions` handling as the standard for container health, as you suggested :)
